title: Doubling, geometric growth and finite sums
transcript: A doubling pattern multiplies the current amount by two each time. Compare it with adding a fixed amount: its increases get larger as the terms grow. To sum a doubling sequence, double the whole sum and align the common terms. Subtract to leave only the two ends.

An AMC problem may use objects that double each day or a prize that grows by a fixed multiplier. Mark whether it asks for one term or a total. In a Mawa style investigation, compare the total with the next term. Changing the starting number scales both.
A display begins with four lights on day one. The number doubles each day. How many are on at day six? Count how many doublings happen after the first day.
There are five doublings. Each one multiplies the current number by two, so use that power of two. Multiply the starting amount by that power. Day six has one hundred and twenty-eight lights.
Find the sum of the first seven terms of the sequence one, two, four, eight and so on. What stays after you double the sum and subtract the original?

Let the whole sum be S. Doubling every term begins at two and ends at one hundred and twenty-eight. Subtract S. Every term shared by the two rows cancels. Only the last term of the doubled row and the first term of the original remain. So the sum is one hundred and twenty-eight minus one, or one hundred and twenty-seven.

A project uses five tokens on day one. Each day's requirement doubles. There are one thousand five hundred and ninety-five tokens in the whole budget. How many complete days can it run? A day counts only if all of its tokens are available.

The total through day n is five times two to the power n minus one, with the minus one inside the multiplier. The total for eight days is one thousand two hundred and seventy-five, which fits the budget. The next total would be two thousand five hundred and fifty-five. The next total is over budget, so there are eight complete days. The unused balance is three hundred and twenty tokens.

After day eight, the amount needed for the next single day is one thousand two hundred and eighty tokens. It exceeds the balance. Every additional day uses positive tokens, so no later stopping point can be cheaper. The two consecutive totals prove the bound.

The value on a day and the amount used across all days are different quantities. Check whether the problem says on or through. Keep the first term when indexing the powers. There are zero doublings at the start.
Find the first term and the repeated multiplier. Mark whether you are calculating a term or a sum. For a budget limit, show the last affordable total and the next one. They prove where you must stop.
